newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan says China defence budget hike shows threat.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan says China defence budget hike shows threat.

text.p: Taiwan's defence minister said on Wednesday that rival China's 1997 defence budget increase was much bigger had been announced and showed that the communist government in Beijing still had ambitions of attacking Taiwan.
Defence Minister Chiang Chung-ling told legislators that China's defence budget for 1997 was at least 2.5 times more than its official increase of 14.7 percent to 80.57 billion yuan ($9.7 billion).

"Communist China's defence budget is not limited to the announced figure. The actual figure is at least 2.5 times the surface figure," Chiang was quoted by the state-run Central News Agency as saying.
"The defence budget increase demonstrates that communist China's ambition to invade Taiwan is still there," Chiang said.
But Chiang denied that Taiwan's decision to resume live-fire missile drills was caused by military and political concerns following the recent death of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping.
"The drills have nothing to do with whether Deng Xiaoping is dead or not," Chiang said. "We would have had the drills even if Deng Xiaoping did not die."
Taiwan's military forces were put on alert after Deng died on February 19.

The ministry cancelled the drills on March 1996 to avoid escalating military tensions with China after Beijing staged menacing war games off Taiwan that triggered the worst military crisis in the Taiwan Strait in decades.

The war games, held in the run-up to Taiwan's presidential elections and after President Lee Teng-hui visited the United States in June 1995, were aimed at intimidating the island for what Beijing saw as moves to promote independence.
China, which has viewed Taiwan as a renegade province since the Nationalists fled there after losing the civil war in 1949, vows to attack the island if it tries to declare independence.
Taiwan has also raised its defence budget in recent years, buying defence weapons to counter China's military advances.
Taiwan's fiscal 1996/97 (July/June) defence spending rose 3.8 percent to a record T$255.3 billion (US$9.3 billion).
Chiang said on Wednesday that first batches of the 60 Mirage fighter jets that Taiwan bought from France and the 150 F-16 fighters bought from the United States in the early 1990s would soon arrive.
"We have already received five planes each from France and the U.S.," Chiang said. "They will begin to arrive in Taiwan after April."

China, which regards any selling of advanced military equipment to Taiwan by foreign powers as an encroachment upon its sphere of sovereignty, had protested vehemently against the F-16 and Mirage deals.
Taipei says the new fighters would enable it to stay ahead of the Chinese air force, despite Beijing's own efforts to upgrade with the purchase of new fighters like the Russian Sukhoi-27.
